subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] I allow this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated November 14, 2019 rejecting her claim for refugee protection on the grounds of a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kenya. I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence concerned, including the entire Appellant's Record and the written transcript of the RPD hearing. In making my decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.1 I have determined the RPD erred in its findings related to the issue of IFA and that there is sufficient evidence to conclude that the Appellant is a Convention2 refugee under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).3
DECISION

[2] The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugees.

The Appellant is a victim of domestic violence within a forced marriage in Kenya to a much older man. Her husband is a wealthy businessman who owns XXXX stores in XXXX, Kenya. Her husband has asked about her whereabouts since she left Kenya and has made threats to harm her if she returns.
NEW EVIDENCE

i. arose after the RPD decision; or
ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.

ANALYSIS

[10] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.7

[11] The RPD found the Appellant to be credible. The sworn testimony of an Appellant is assumed to be truthful unless the presumption is rebutted.8 I have examined all the evidence and have reviewed the written transcript of the hearing. After doing so, I find no inconsistencies or material omissions within the Appellant's sworn testimony or her Basis of Claim form.

[12] I therefore accept the allegations made by the Appellant. I find she has a subjective fear of being pursued and harmed by her husband. Given the high prevalence of domestic abuse by husbands against their wives in Kenya, and that I have accepted the Appellant's allegations, I find there is an objective basis for the Appellant's fears.
Internal flight alternative

[13] The RPD identified three possible IFA locations in its decision.

[14] The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:9
a. The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA.
b. Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.
The husband has the motivation and means: The IFA is not safe

[15] The RPD found that the Appellant's concern that her husband could find her in the IFA was vague and speculative, and that there was insufficient evidence to establish that her husband would be able to locate her if she were to relocate to a different part of the country.

[16] The RPD made no finding regarding the motivation of the Appellant's husband and whether he maintained any ongoing interest in her. The Appellant testified that she has remained in touch with her mother and sister in Kenya who tell her that her husband has been saying that when he finds her "she will know who I am"10 meaning that he will harm her. There is a recent letter I have accepted as new evidence from the Appellant's sister in Kenya who states as follows: "I have seen the way her husband used to treat her so badly up to now he still comes to the house and ask for his wife and threatened us that when he finds her his going to kill her to be honest his really a violent man not someone to be trusted at all."11

[17] Based on this evidence, I am satisfied that the husband maintains a forward looking interest in the Appellant, and given the past abusive behaviour would likely be abusive towards her in the future. I agree with the Appellant's submission that if anything, the abuse may escalate given that the Appellant has left him.

[18] Regarding means, the RPD found that the Appellant had not established that her husband by himself had the means to locate her if she moved to one of the proposed IFAs. The RPD found nothing in the Appellant's testimony to indicate that her husband had nationwide influence and she was unable to articulate how her husband would find her using the influences he had with the police or other wealthy business associates.

[19] The Appellant submits that the RPD's analysis was unreasonable as it expected that a young uneducated woman in an abusive relationship, navigating life in a forced marriage, would recognize that it was incumbent on her to know and remember significant and substantive details about her husband's clout in the police force or with other influential individuals. Further, the documentary evidence is clear that police corruption in Kenya is widespread. As well, it is submitted that the RPD ignored the Appellant's husband's profile as a wealthy and prominent elder businessman living in a patriarchal Kenyan society that is predominantly controlled by men with a similar profile.

[20] In the circumstances of this case, which involve an uneducated young woman who lived entirely under the protection of her father, followed by an influential and wealthy abusive husband, I find that it is not unusual or unexpected that the Appellant should not be able to recall or share specific details regarding how her husband might locate her. I have also considered Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Prosecution, which highlights the fact that in certain cultures and circumstances women may not be privy to details about their husband's activities.12 As the RPD found no reason to doubt the Appellant's credibility, I accept that the husband's profile as a wealthy elderly businessman who possesses a motivation to seek out the Appellant who abandoned him, along with the widespread prevalence of police corruption, would allow him the means to search for and find the Appellant in one of the IFA locations. Thus, I find more than a mere possibility exists that the husband has the means to find the Appellant in the IFA locations.

[21] As I find that the husband does have the motivation and means to locate her and harm her in the IFAs, this IFA therefore fails the first prong of the test.
The internal flight alternative is not reasonable

[22] As the first part of the IFA test fails, there is no need to analyze the second part in detail. That said, I find that the second part of the IFA test also fails. Generally, the documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) discusses conditions for women in Nairobi; however, I infer that the challenges outlined also relate to relocating to other places in Kenya. Even if the husband could not locate her in one of the IFA locations, I find that it would be unreasonable for the following reasons.

[23] In my view, there are several significant aspects of the Appellant's profile that warrant consideration in the test for reasonableness of the IFAs. First, the Appellant would be returning to the IFA as a single woman. The documentary evidence is clear that single women in Kenya face challenges living alone in Kenya. The rate of gender-based violence is high.13 Second, the Appellant is a survivor of gender-based violence, which carries its own stigma.14 Third, she is largely uneducated and has no formal work history. Fourth, there is some degree of ethnic friction between Kenyans of Somali ethnicity, which is the background of the Appellant, and indigenous ethnic groups. The Appellant testified that as a Somali she experienced discrimination based on her Somalian identity. Fifth, the Appellant lived entirely under the protection of first her father and family and then an abusive, influential husband. Sixth, other than one friend in Nairobi, the Appellant has no familial relationships in any of the IFA locations. Given these elements of her profile, I find that it more likely that as a single female without male guardianship or familial support she would face a higher likelihood of gender and ethnic discrimination upon her return to Kenya would impacts reasonableness. The cumulative impact of an Appellant's particular circumstances must be considered in the test for reasonableness.15

[24] Further, I find that employment is precarious, unstable, and difficult for the Appellant to obtain in the IFA locations. The objective evidence in item 5.5 of the NDP indicates that women face discrimination in accessing credit and they are concentrated in the informal sector, which is characterized by low wages, menial jobs that are available erratically, and a reliance on referrals through one's social or informal networks, which exposes women to a high risk of abuse and violence. The Appellant has no family members in any of the IFA locations, placing her in a vulnerable position as a woman who would be new to the city, and exposed to gender-based discrimination, ethnic discrimination, and sexual violence.16 Further, item 5.5 states that widows may engage in sex-work to make a living in Nairobi,17 and as a lone, uneducated, unmarried woman undertaking forced re-location to an IFA, the Appellant is similarly situated to widows in her vulnerability to life-threatening or degrading work to support herself because, like the widow, she also does not have a husband. Further, while the Appellant has been attempting to upgrade her education in Canada, her Schedule A indicates that she has completed seven years of primary school only.18 With this level of education, and a previous work history she testified to only consisted of domestic work which produced no real income, she may be forced into work such as street vending. The objective information from the NDP suggests that street vending places women at risk of daily harassment and abuse.

argument_evidence.context_text: [25] Although the courts have set a high bar for finding a proposed IFA to be unreasonable, I find that this bar has been met in the Appellant's specific situation.
[26] The objective documentary evidence states that there is widespread impunity for perpetrators of domestic violence.

Although there are some laws to protect survivors of domestic violence, there are also a number of obstacles that prevent women from accessing justice, including poverty, lack of knowledge or support, and patriarchal and misguided interpretation of the law.

[27] After reviewing the country conditions for survivors of domestic violence in Kenya, I find clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of state protection and that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming in this particular case.

[27] After reviewing the country conditions for survivors of domestic violence in Kenya, I find clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of state protection and that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming in this particular case.

[25] Although the courts have set a high bar for finding a proposed IFA to be unreasonable, I find that this bar has been met in the Appellant's specific situation. This analysis of the appropriateness of the IFA is linked to the guideline on women claimants and applied to the particular case of this Kenyan woman to consider how she would be affected in her own circumstances. The Appellant would face significant hardship in finding employment and housing. Without employment, the Appellant would face poverty. As the test for an IFA fails on the second prong, I also find that there is no viable IFA for the Appellant anywhere in Kenya.
State protection

[26] The objective documentary evidence states that there is widespread impunity for perpetrators of domestic violence. Police may accept bribes from perpetrators in order to avoid being brought to justice. Although there are some laws to protect survivors of domestic violence, there are also a number of obstacles that prevent women from accessing justice, including poverty, lack of knowledge or support, and patriarchal and misguided interpretation of the law.19

[27] After reviewing the country conditions for survivors of domestic violence in Kenya, I find clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of state protection and that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming in this particular case.

[28] In conclusion, considering that the Appellant has been found to be credible, that there is no state protection or IFA for her, I find that she has established a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] I allow this appeal. XXXX XXXX XXXX (Appellant) is a citizen of Kenya who is appealing a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) dated November 14, 2019 rejecting her claim for refugee protection on the grounds of a viable Internal Flight Alternative (IFA) in Kenya. I have conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence concerned, including the entire Appellant's Record and the written transcript of the RPD hearing. In making my decision, I have considered and applied the Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Persecution.1 I have determined the RPD erred in its findings related to the issue of IFA and that there is sufficient evidence to conclude that the Appellant is a Convention2 refugee under section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).3
DECISION
[2] The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugees.
BACKGROUND

[3] These are the allegations of the Appellant which the RPD accepted to be credible. I also accept the truth of the following. The Appellant is a victim of domestic violence within a forced marriage in Kenya to a much older man. Her husband is a wealthy businessman who owns XXXX stores in XXXX, Kenya. Her husband has asked about her whereabouts since she left Kenya and has made threats to harm her if she returns.
NEW EVIDENCE

[4] The evidence presented by the Appellant is accepted. The Appellant sought to enter one document as new evidence, namely a letter from the Appellant's sister, XXXX XXXX XXXX, in Kenya dated XXXX XXXX, 2019 along with identity documentation for the author.

[5] According to the law,4 I can only accept evidence that:
i. arose after the RPD decision; or
ii. was not reasonably available at the time of the decision; or
iii. that you could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to bring to the RPD before the decision.
[6] If the evidence meets one or more of these requirements, I must decide if the evidence is new, credible and relevant before I can accept it.5

[7] The Appellant submits that the letter is admissible as it describes the Appellant's husband's demanding, threatening and possessive behaviour since the RPD rendered its decision and is both relevant and probative as it corroborates that risk is ongoing.

[8] As the contents of the letter describe the agent of persecution's conduct, which arose after the RPD decision, is new and both relevant and probative, I will enter this letter into evidence.
RPD Decision

[9] The RPD found that the Appellant was credible, but that both prongs of the test for an IFA in Nairobi, Kisumu or Nakuru were satisfied, and accordingly the Appellant's claim failed under both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.6
ANALYSIS
[10] My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.7

[11] The RPD found the Appellant to be credible. The sworn testimony of an Appellant is assumed to be truthful unless the presumption is rebutted.8 I have examined all the evidence and have reviewed the written transcript of the hearing. After doing so, I find no inconsistencies or material omissions within the Appellant's sworn testimony or her Basis of Claim form.

[12] I therefore accept the allegations made by the Appellant. I find she has a subjective fear of being pursued and harmed by her husband. Given the high prevalence of domestic abuse by husbands against their wives in Kenya, and that I have accepted the Appellant's allegations, I find there is an objective basis for the Appellant's fears.
Internal flight alternative
[13] The RPD identified three possible IFA locations in its decision.

[14] The test for assessing an IFA is two-pronged and is set out in the Federal Court of Appeal decision in Rasaratnam:9
a. The Board must be satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA.
b. Moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.
The husband has the motivation and means: The IFA is not safe

[15] The RPD found that the Appellant's concern that her husband could find her in the IFA was vague and speculative, and that there was insufficient evidence to establish that her husband would be able to locate her if she were to relocate to a different part of the country.

[16] The RPD made no finding regarding the motivation of the Appellant's husband and whether he maintained any ongoing interest in her. The Appellant testified that she has remained in touch with her mother and sister in Kenya who tell her that her husband has been saying that when he finds her "she will know who I am"10 meaning that he will harm her. There is a recent letter I have accepted as new evidence from the Appellant's sister in Kenya who states as follows: "I have seen the way her husband used to treat her so badly up to now he still comes to the house and ask for his wife and threatened us that when he finds her his going to kill her to be honest his really a violent man not someone to be trusted at all."11

[17] Based on this evidence, I am satisfied that the husband maintains a forward looking interest in the Appellant, and given the past abusive behaviour would likely be abusive towards her in the future. I agree with the Appellant's submission that if anything, the abuse may escalate given that the Appellant has left him.

[18] Regarding means, the RPD found that the Appellant had not established that her husband by himself had the means to locate her if she moved to one of the proposed IFAs. The RPD found nothing in the Appellant's testimony to indicate that her husband had nationwide influence and she was unable to articulate how her husband would find her using the influences he had with the police or other wealthy business associates.

[19] The Appellant submits that the RPD's analysis was unreasonable as it expected that a young uneducated woman in an abusive relationship, navigating life in a forced marriage, would recognize that it was incumbent on her to know and remember significant and substantive details about her husband's clout in the police force or with other influential individuals. Further, the documentary evidence is clear that police corruption in Kenya is widespread. As well, it is submitted that the RPD ignored the Appellant's husband's profile as a wealthy and prominent elder businessman living in a patriarchal Kenyan society that is predominantly controlled by men with a similar profile.

[20] In the circumstances of this case, which involve an uneducated young woman who lived entirely under the protection of her father, followed by an influential and wealthy abusive husband, I find that it is not unusual or unexpected that the Appellant should not be able to recall or share specific details regarding how her husband might locate her. I have also considered Chairperson's Guideline 4: Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender-Related Prosecution, which highlights the fact that in certain cultures and circumstances women may not be privy to details about their husband's activities.12 As the RPD found no reason to doubt the Appellant's credibility, I accept that the husband's profile as a wealthy elderly businessman who possesses a motivation to seek out the Appellant who abandoned him, along with the widespread prevalence of police corruption, would allow him the means to search for and find the Appellant in one of the IFA locations. Thus, I find more than a mere possibility exists that the husband has the means to find the Appellant in the IFA locations.

[21] As I find that the husband does have the motivation and means to locate her and harm her in the IFAs, this IFA therefore fails the first prong of the test.
The internal flight alternative is not reasonable

[22] As the first part of the IFA test fails, there is no need to analyze the second part in detail. That said, I find that the second part of the IFA test also fails. Generally, the documentary evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP) discusses conditions for women in Nairobi; however, I infer that the challenges outlined also relate to relocating to other places in Kenya. Even if the husband could not locate her in one of the IFA locations, I find that it would be unreasonable for the following reasons.

[23] In my view, there are several significant aspects of the Appellant's profile that warrant consideration in the test for reasonableness of the IFAs. First, the Appellant would be returning to the IFA as a single woman. The documentary evidence is clear that single women in Kenya face challenges living alone in Kenya. The rate of gender-based violence is high.13 Second, the Appellant is a survivor of gender-based violence, which carries its own stigma.14 Third, she is largely uneducated and has no formal work history. Fourth, there is some degree of ethnic friction between Kenyans of Somali ethnicity, which is the background of the Appellant, and indigenous ethnic groups. The Appellant testified that as a Somali she experienced discrimination based on her Somalian identity. Fifth, the Appellant lived entirely under the protection of first her father and family and then an abusive, influential husband. Sixth, other than one friend in Nairobi, the Appellant has no familial relationships in any of the IFA locations. Given these elements of her profile, I find that it more likely that as a single female without male guardianship or familial support she would face a higher likelihood of gender and ethnic discrimination upon her return to Kenya would impacts reasonableness. The cumulative impact of an Appellant's particular circumstances must be considered in the test for reasonableness.15

[24] Further, I find that employment is precarious, unstable, and difficult for the Appellant to obtain in the IFA locations. The objective evidence in item 5.5 of the NDP indicates that women face discrimination in accessing credit and they are concentrated in the informal sector, which is characterized by low wages, menial jobs that are available erratically, and a reliance on referrals through one's social or informal networks, which exposes women to a high risk of abuse and violence. The Appellant has no family members in any of the IFA locations, placing her in a vulnerable position as a woman who would be new to the city, and exposed to gender-based discrimination, ethnic discrimination, and sexual violence.16 Further, item 5.5 states that widows may engage in sex-work to make a living in Nairobi,17 and as a lone, uneducated, unmarried woman undertaking forced re-location to an IFA, the Appellant is similarly situated to widows in her vulnerability to life-threatening or degrading work to support herself because, like the widow, she also does not have a husband. Further, while the Appellant has been attempting to upgrade her education in Canada, her Schedule A indicates that she has completed seven years of primary school only.18 With this level of education, and a previous work history she testified to only consisted of domestic work which produced no real income, she may be forced into work such as street vending. The objective information from the NDP suggests that street vending places women at risk of daily harassment and abuse.

[25] Although the courts have set a high bar for finding a proposed IFA to be unreasonable, I find that this bar has been met in the Appellant's specific situation. This analysis of the appropriateness of the IFA is linked to the guideline on women claimants and applied to the particular case of this Kenyan woman to consider how she would be affected in her own circumstances. The Appellant would face significant hardship in finding employment and housing. Without employment, the Appellant would face poverty. As the test for an IFA fails on the second prong, I also find that there is no viable IFA for the Appellant anywhere in Kenya.
State protection

[26] The objective documentary evidence states that there is widespread impunity for perpetrators of domestic violence. Police may accept bribes from perpetrators in order to avoid being brought to justice. Although there are some laws to protect survivors of domestic violence, there are also a number of obstacles that prevent women from accessing justice, including poverty, lack of knowledge or support, and patriarchal and misguided interpretation of the law.19

[27] After reviewing the country conditions for survivors of domestic violence in Kenya, I find clear and convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of state protection and that adequate state protection would not be reasonably forthcoming in this particular case.

[28] In conclusion, considering that the Appellant has been found to be credible, that there is no state protection or IFA for her, I find that she has established a well-founded fear of persecution under section 96 of the IRPA.
CONCLUSION

[29] The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellant is a Convention refugee.
(signed)
Kim Polowek
